To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) large-scale tree plantations can impose externalities on downstream irrigation, wetland and stock and domestic users; (ii) the value of these externalities depends on the value of the first GL of water to be used by downstream parties; and (iii) a policy requiring upstream tree planters to purchase permanent water entitlements from downstream parties before planting can reduce these externalities, but only if the price is set to reflect the value of the water to downstream users.

the upstream demand for water use by new tree plantations in the Macquarie River sub-catchment, in the absence of a water entitlement purchase policy, imposes externalities on downstream irrigated agriculture and wetlands.

(a) large-scale plantation forestry in high rainfall areas can impose externalities on downstream irrigators and other water users; (b) the value of water to irrigators is greater than the value of water for forestry, so downstream users should be compensated if upstream plantations are established, and (c) compensation can be achieved by requiring upstream water users to purchase permanent water entitlements from downstream water users, prior to establishing plantations.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the value of water is much greater for agriculture and forestry than it is for the environment, but that this is a misleading statement.
the external cost of plantation water use is not a large fraction of the economic value of water to agriculture and wetlands, but it is not trivial.
, while the net benefits of tree plantations are positive in the absence of a water purchase requirement, they are much reduced by a requirement to purchase downstream water entitlements.
The main takeaway from our work is that
water use externalities can be expressed in terms of the same unit as water itself, and that this provides an effective basis for assessing the costs and benefits of water use by competing uses.
the water market, in which downstream water users can purchase water entitlements from upstream parties, provides a mechanism to internalize these externalities.
